planting.note: Plant bulbs 5-6 inches deep once soil has warmed after the last frost, in a sheltered spot out of strong wind.

directions: This South African relative of the more familiar summer hyacinth is taller and earlier to bloom, sending up thick spikes from late June into July rather than late summer. The waxy, pendulous bells are greenish-white with a darker central band running down each petal, held in a denser, more compact raceme than the open spikes of the common summer hyacinth. Plant in rich, well-drained soil in full sun and stake tall spikes in exposed gardens, since the flowering stem can outgrow its own support. Where winters drop much below zone 8, lift bulbs in fall and store them dry and frost-free over winter, replanting after the ground has warmed in spring.

common_name: Barberton Belladonna Lily (Dark Pink Naked Lady)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in summer or early fall with the neck at or just above the soil surface; withhold water during summer dormancy before the leafless flower stalks emerge.

directions: 'Barberton' is a deep rose-pink to carmine selection of the belladonna lily, chosen for flower color intensity rather than any change in habit, so it keeps the species' tall, leafless stalks and strappy winter foliage that dies back before the bare summer dormancy. Its trumpet-shaped blooms run larger than the typical pale pink species form and cluster densely atop each stem, making a bolder statement at the back of a dry border or along a sunny foundation planting. Grow it exactly as you would any belladonna lily, in lean, fast-draining soil in full sun, and resist the temptation to water during the dormant summer months, which can rot the bulb or delay flowering. Established clumps are long-lived and best left undisturbed for years, increasing slowly by offsets.

subcategory: tender tropical bulb grown as a houseplant

planting.note: Pot bulbs with the neck at the soil surface in spring; grow outdoors only in frost-free climates, otherwise keep as a warm greenhouse or houseplant specimen year-round.

directions: Eucharis moorei carries noticeably larger, more substantial flowers than the commonly grown Amazon lily hybrids, with broad white star-shaped blooms held well above glossy, peace-lily-like foliage and a strong sweet fragrance that fills a room. Keep it in bright, indirect light rather than direct sun, which scorches the thin-textured leaves, and maintain warm, draft-free temperatures and even moisture for best flowering. Like other Eucharis, it dislikes being disturbed and flowers most reliably when slightly pot-bound, so repot infrequently and only when the clump has clearly outgrown its container. Allow a brief, cooler, slightly drier rest between flowering cycles to help trigger the next round of bloom.

subcategory: tender South African daisy hybrid grown as a warm-season bedding perennial

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or nursery plugs around the last frost date once the soil has warmed; in zones 9-11 it can be left in place as a short-lived perennial.

directions: 'Pink Sugar' is a hybrid African daisy derived from crosses between Arctotis venusta and Arctotis fastuosa, bred for a compact mounding habit rather than the taller, looser growth of the species parents. Soft pink petals surround a warm orange-yellow eye above felted, silvery-gray foliage, and the plant flowers nearly continuously from spring through fall wherever nights stay mild. Because it is a named hybrid selection, propagate by cuttings rather than seed to keep plants true to type, and give it the same lean, sharply drained soil and full sun that any silver-leaved Arctotis demands. Shear lightly after the first big flush to tidy the plant and encourage continued branching and bloom.

planting.note: Start seeds indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost and transplant out after frost into a dry, sunny, very well-drained site.

directions: 'Major' is a selected form of cupid's dart with larger, more richly colored lavender-blue ray flowers surrounding a sharply contrasting deep purple center, a combination that has earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. It shares the straight species' papery, everlasting-type bud scales and wiry upright stems, making it just as useful for cutting and drying, but with noticeably bigger blooms held slightly taller. Grow it exactly as you would ordinary cupid's dart, in lean, fast-draining, sun-baked soil that mimics its native Mediterranean hillsides, since damp or heavy ground quickly rots the crown. Deadhead and shear lightly after the first flush to prolong bloom, and treat as short-lived, replacing or allowing self-sown seedlings to refresh the planting every few years.

planting.note: Start seed indoors in late summer for fall transplanting, or set out purchased transplants in early fall for winter and spring bloom in mild climates.

directions: Habanera is a seed-grown English daisy series bred by the German seed house Ernst Benary, producing fully double, 2-inch flower heads with narrow, quilled petals that give the blooms a fluffier, shaggier look than the rounder, button-form Pomponette series. It comes in a mix of red, pink, and white shades on compact, low plants well suited to spring bedding, edging, and containers. Give it the same cool, moist, humus-rich soil and part-shade to full-sun exposure that any English daisy needs, since hot, dry conditions quickly end its bloom cycle and bring on decline. In mild winter climates it flowers over an extended cool season, while in colder zones it is best grown as a fall-sown biennial for a single spring flush.

planting.note: Plant divisions or potted rhizomes in spring into permanently damp, humus-rich soil at a pond margin or bog garden.

directions: Unlike its giant South American relatives, this is the only Gunnera native to Africa, forming a much smaller clump of mottled, rhubarb-like leaves topped in late summer by a distinctive dense, purple-brown flower spike. It is traditionally known in South Africa as river pumpkin for its role in ethnomedicine, but in gardens it earns its place as a tidy, smaller-scale marginal or bog plant where the larger Gunnera species would overwhelm the space. Keep the soil constantly wet, as at a pond edge, stream bank, or rain garden, and provide full sun to light shade; it will not tolerate drying out even briefly. In climates colder than about zone 8, mulch the crown heavily for winter or lift and overwinter divisions under cover.
